findings.title: New order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is loaded via ServiceLoader and can be implemented outside this repository. Adding `int order()` as a non-default interface method breaks source and binary compatibility for existing providers: older implementations will fail to compile against the new API and may throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when CryptoIntegration sorts them. A default method should be provided instead.

findings.title: Multiple providers with equal order are selected silently and non-deterministically
findings.body: detectProvider now loads all registered CryptoProviders, sorts them by order descending, and returns the first one. All full providers in this PR return the same order (200), so if more than one real provider is present (for example default and FIPS/Elytron), the selected provider depends on ServiceLoader/classpath ordering. The previous fail-fast behavior was removed and ignored providers are only debug-logged. This can silently select an unintended crypto provider, with security-sensitive consequences. Consider failing on ties for the highest order, or at least logging a warning and assigning distinct orders.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an arbitrary keystore provider
findings.body: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider returns the provider of a default KeyStore instance. The CryptoProvider contract asks for the BouncyCastle security provider, but this code may return any JCA provider depending on the JVM configuration. Callers that rely on the returned provider name or capabilities may fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException or use an unintended provider. An explicit fallback should be used instead of repurposing a keystore provider.

findings.title: Indefinite-length ASN.1 values are not handled safely
findings.body: readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, but callers do not support this value. readSequence will silently stop parsing, while readInteger/readNext can end up passing a negative or otherwise invalid length to read(int), causing NegativeArraySizeException or reading incorrect bytes. Malformed ASN.1 input should be rejected with IOException rather than causing undefined behavior.

findings.title: Zero-length INTEGER causes NumberFormatException instead of IOException
findings.body: readInteger reads the length and then constructs a BigInteger from the read bytes. If a malformed DER INTEGER has length 0, `new BigInteger(bytes)` throws NumberFormatException, an unchecked exception, instead of the IOException used for other ASN.1 parsing failures. The parser should validate that the integer length is positive and throw IOException for malformed input.

findings.title: integerToBytes silently discards leading bytes of oversized coordinates
findings.body: In the ECDSA conversion, when BigInteger.toByteArray() returns more bytes than the expected coordinate length, integerToBytes copies only the last qLength bytes without verifying that the discarded leading bytes are zero. A valid positive integer may be one byte longer due to a DER sign byte, but a larger or corrupted value will be silently truncated, producing an incorrect concatenated R/S signature. The method should reject oversized values or verify that all dropped bytes are zero.

findings.title: ECDSA tests do not use algorithm-appropriate curves or verify signatures
findings.body: The test generates a default EC key pair and uses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512, so the larger algorithms are not exercised with their expected curves or key sizes. It also only checks that concatenated R/S values round-trip through the converter; it never verifies that the DER-encoded signature produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is accepted by Signature.verify, nor does it cover edge cases such as coordinates with leading zeros or the high bit set. Add curve-specific key generation and signature verification tests.
